There are quite some reasons why you would shoot something with your smartphone, not your mirrorless or DSLR camera. First of all, of course is if you don't have any other camera gear and all you have is your smartphone and you just love taking photos with it. Second thing is that smartphone is always at hands, so if something unexpected comes, you can always take it out and shoot some photos. Another reason is that people will find it less intimidating if you point your cell phone to them instead of a big camera with a huge lens on it. Another situation where mobile phones can be very handy are locations where big DSLR cameras are not allowed but you can always have your phone with you. So let's check which those are, and let's talk about some things that you have to take into consideration when shooting with your mobile phone. Most of this limitations come from the size as the camera sensor. Because of the size of the smartphone of course, camera sensors in these devices are very small. Compared to a full frame sensor in a professional cameras, for example smart, camera sensors in these devices are very very small compared to a full-frame sensor in a professional camera for example, smartphone camera sensor are around 50 times smaller Let me tell you about the consequences of that The first thing is low-light performance of course, if the light is good, if you're shooting in bright daylight conditions images shot on smartphones can look great but as soon as the light quality is lower you'll see the weakness of a small sensor. In low-light smartphones have two options. One, is to increase ISO which will result in grainy images, especially on small sensors like those in smartphones. Even if we increase ISO by a small amount, it can introduce a lot of grain to your image. Or the other thing it can do is to extend shutter time and the result of that can Be a blurry image. So native camera apps can have some tools to enhance your low-light images like noise reduction But if there's too much noise reduction applied your image can look even worse You can avoid that to some degree by using some apps and shooting in raw But let's leave that for next week's video So be sure to come back to watch it so my first advice for shooting with your phone is try to get as much light as Possible and try to avoid very dark scenes. Okay, let's move to the second thing, which is dynamic range So the more dynamic range the camera has more details There will be in the darkest and the brightest areas of an image smartphone cameras are not one of those devices with high dynamic range that's why if you're shooting something in the shadow on a sunny day the sky in the background will be overexposed usually without any details in it. You can avoid it by underexposing your image and brightening shadow parts in post, but when you do that there will be a lot of noise in those shadowed areas But when I'm shooting the same scene with my full-frame camera I can under expose an image quite a lot leave the shadows in post-production and the image will be totally fine So my second advice is in contrast these scenes decide which part of an image is more important Highlights or shadows and expose the image with that in mind So if the shadow areas are important and expose the image with that in mind. But if the sky is important, then underexpose shadow areas so the sky will be exposed correctly. Next thing that's connected to a small camera sensor is the depth of field. If you're shooting with your phone everything will be sharp. You can't get that nice background blur or bokeh that you can get with a full-frame camera. Of course, most phones these days have portrait mode where you can blur the background. But the only thing portrait mode is good for are portraits. In that case it can work great but also there it can be weird on the edges. And for example, you can't use burst mode in combination with portrait mode so just try to capture a biker riding a bike towards you I don't think you'll be very successful at that and one more phone camera limitation that's not connected to camera sensor are lenses on smartphones you can have 1 2 or 3 different focal lengths and you're limited on using those so you can can shoot an object from a long distance for example. But with a DSLR or mirrorless camera you have a ton of options. You can choose between wide, narrow, telephoto, macro, tilt shift lenses and so on. So yes smartphone cameras are very convenient and can take great photos and videos and you can make some money with those, but you have to have those limitations in mind when you're shooting.
